items.title: Identifying Quadric Surfaces and Cylinders

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at [MATH: O] is given by

[MATH: z = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2},]

and a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at [MATH: (x_0,y_0,z_0)] is given by

[MATH: z - z_0 = \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2}.]

Thus, our equation is a hyperbolic paraboloid with the following parameters:

[MATH: (x_0,y_0,z_0) = (3, -2, 1), \quad a= b=2.]

items.title: Identifying Quadric Surfaces and Cylinders With Alternative Orientations

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at [MATH: O] whose axis of symmetry is the [MATH: z]-axis is given by

[MATH: z = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}.]

Thus, a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at [MATH: O] whose axis of symmetry is the [MATH: \boldsymbol x]-axis is given by

[MATH: x = \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}.]

Therefore, our equation is a hyperbolic paraboloid whose axis of symmetry is the [MATH: x]-axis, and [MATH: b=2, \: c=\dfrac 12.]

items.title: Identifying Quadric Surfaces by Completing the Square

sections.normalized_html:
First, we complete the square in the [MATH: x] term:

[MATH: − x^{2} + z^{2} + 2x + y|= 0; − (x^{2} − 2x) + z^{2} + y|= 0; − (x − 1)^{2} + 1 + z^{2} + y|= 0]

Now, by rearranging, we get the equation

[MATH: − (x − 1)^{2} + 1 + z^{2} + y|= 0; − (x − 1)^{2} + z^{2}|= − y − 1; (x − 1)^{2} − z^{2}|= y + 1.]

This is the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at [MATH: (1, -1, 0).]
sections.readable_text:
First, we complete the square in the [MATH: x] term:

[MATH: − x^{2} + z^{2} + 2x + y|= 0; − (x^{2} − 2x) + z^{2} + y|= 0; − (x − 1)^{2} + 1 + z^{2} + y|= 0]

Now, by rearranging, we get the equation

[MATH: − (x − 1)^{2} + 1 + z^{2} + y|= 0; − (x − 1)^{2} + z^{2}|= − y − 1; (x − 1)^{2} − z^{2}|= y + 1.]

This is the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at [MATH: (1, -1, 0).]

Example Prompt:
Identify the surface [MATH: -x^2 + z^2 + 2x + y=0.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we complete the square in the [MATH: x] term:

[MATH: − x^{2} + z^{2} + 2x + y|= 0; − (x^{2} − 2x) + z^{2} + y|= 0; − (x − 1)^{2} + 1 + z^{2} + y|= 0]

Now, by rearranging, we get the equation

[MATH: − (x − 1)^{2} + 1 + z^{2} + y|= 0; − (x − 1)^{2} + z^{2}|= − y − 1; (x − 1)^{2} − z^{2}|= y + 1.]

This is the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at [MATH: (1, -1, 0).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Recall that the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at [MATH: O] is given by

[MATH: z = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2},]

and a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at [MATH: (x_0,y_0,z_0)] is given by

[MATH: z - z_0 = \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2}.]

Thus, our equation is a hyperbolic paraboloid with the following parameters:

Item 6 — Example: Identifying Quadric Surfaces and Cylinders With Alternative Orientations

Example Prompt:

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at [MATH: O] whose axis of symmetry is the [MATH: z]-axis is given by

[MATH: z = \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}.]

Thus, a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at [MATH: O] whose axis of symmetry is the [MATH: \boldsymbol x]-axis is given by

[MATH: x = \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} - \dfrac{z^2}{c^2}.]

Therefore, our equation is a hyperbolic paraboloid whose axis of symmetry is the [MATH: x]-axis, and [MATH: b=2, \: c=\dfrac 12.]

Item 9 — Example: Identifying Quadric Surfaces by Completing the Square

Example Prompt:
Identify the surface [MATH: -x^2 + z^2 + 2x + y=0.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we complete the square in the [MATH: x] term:

[MATH: − x^{2} + z^{2} + 2x + y|= 0; − (x^{2} − 2x) + z^{2} + y|= 0; − (x − 1)^{2} + 1 + z^{2} + y|= 0]

Now, by rearranging, we get the equation

[MATH: − (x − 1)^{2} + 1 + z^{2} + y|= 0; − (x − 1)^{2} + z^{2}|= − y − 1; (x − 1)^{2} − z^{2}|= y + 1.]

This is the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at [MATH: (1, -1, 0).]
